1.title: Threats, Actors, Motivations and Vulnerability Scoring
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Threats, Actors, Motivations and Vulnerability Scoring. It covers the exam area Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. two point one Explain characteristics of threats and vulnerabilities. two point two Describe common threat actors and motivations. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks (twenty-four percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Threats and vulnerabilities
1.text: Threats and vulnerabilities. Threat. Meaning: Something that could cause harm. Example: A ransomware group. Vulnerability. Meaning: A weakness that a threat can use. Example: An unpatched server. Risk. Meaning: The chance and impact of a threat using a vulnerability. Example: Likelihood times impact.

1.title: Characteristics of threats
1.text: Characteristics of threats. Threat feeds. Streams of indicators and attack data (bad I P addresses, hashes, domains). Likelihood. How probable the event is. Impact. How bad the result would be. Intelligence sources. Where the information comes from: open source (oh sint), proprietary or commercial, industry sharing groups (I sacks), government, and the dark web. Life cycle. Threat information is collected, analyzed, shared and acted on and then reviewed.

1.title: Characteristics of vulnerabilities
1.text: Characteristics of vulnerabilities. Scoring (C V S S). The Common Vulnerability Scoring System rates severity from zero point zero to ten point zero. C V E. Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a unique identifier for a publicly known flaw (for example C V E-two thousand twenty-five to twelve thousand three hundred forty-five). Prioritization. Fix first what is severe, exploitable, exposed and on critical assets. Vulnerability types. Software flaws, misconfigurations, weak credentials, missing patches, design flaws (module six). zero point zero. None. zero point one to three point nine. Low. four point zero to six point nine. Medium. seven point zero to eight point nine. High. nine point zero to ten point zero. Critical.

1.title: Characteristics of vulnerabilities, continued
1.text: Characteristics of vulnerabilities. The figure shows this: C V S S score bands from none to critical. Exam tip: C V E is the name of a flaw; C V S S is its severity score. A critical score alone does not set priority: also weigh exploit availability, exposure and asset value. Likelihood times impact gives risk.

1.title: Threat actors
1.text: Threat actors. Unskilled attacker (script kiddie). Who: A beginner who uses ready-made tools. Typical traits: Low skill, low resources; curiosity or notoriety. Hacktivist. Who: Attacks for a cause. Typical traits: Defacement, leaks, D dos (distributed denial of service); ideological or political. Organized crime or crime syndicate. Who: A criminal group. Typical traits: Financial: ransomware, fraud; good resources. State-sponsored (nation-state). Who: Backed by a government. Typical traits: Espionage, political, disruption; high skill and funding; A P T.

1.title: Threat actors, continued
1.text: Threat actors. Insider. Who: Employee or contractor with access. Typical traits: Revenge, financial; hard to detect. Accidental or unintentional. Who: A well-meaning person who makes a mistake. Typical traits: Misdirected email, misconfiguration. Competitor. Who: A rival business. Typical traits: Intellectual property, advantage. Terrorist. Who: Violent extremists. Typical traits: Fear, chaos, ideology.

1.title: Motivations
1.text: Motivations. Financial, influence, intellectual property, notoriety, espionage, fear and chaos, extortion, general curiosity, revenge, ideological, political, and ethical (for example some researchers).

1.title: Attributes of actors
1.text: Attributes of actors. Internal versus external. Inside the organization or outside. Resources and funding. Money, tools and people available. Level of sophistication and capability. Skill and ability to hide and persist. Exam tip: An insider already has legitimate access, so least privilege, monitoring and separation of duties are the best controls. Shadow I T and mistakes also create insider-type risk.

1.title: Attributes of actors, continued
1.text: Attributes of actors. The figure shows this: Threat actors compared by skill, resources and typical motive. Exam tip: Match actor to motive: money equals organized crime; cause equals hacktivist; long, quiet, well-funded equals state-sponsored; grudge with access equals insider; mistake equals accidental; beginner with tools equals unskilled attacker.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors reads that a vendor flaw has the identifier C V E-two thousand twenty-five to twelve thousand three hundred forty-five and a score of nine point eight. What does the nine point eight represent? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The C V S S severity score, in the critical range. C V S S rates severity from zero to ten, and nine point zero to ten point zero is critical. The C V E is the identifier.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A group encrypts a hospital's files and demands payment. Which threat actor and motivation fit best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Organized crime with financial motivation. Ransomware for payment is typical of organized crime, driven by money.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A well-funded group quietly stays inside a government network for months to steal secrets. Which actor is most likely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: State-sponsored actor. Long-term, well-resourced espionage is typical of state-sponsored actors using advanced persistent threats.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An employee who was passed over for promotion copies customer data before leaving. Which motivation fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Revenge. An insider acting from a grudge is driven by revenge, possibly with a financial motive too.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A security team subscribes to a stream of known malicious I P addresses and file hashes. What are they using? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A threat feed. A threat feed delivers indicators that can be loaded into security tools.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A vulnerability scores seven point five on a minor test server and six point eight on the public payment system. What should the team consider besides the score? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Asset value, exposure and exploitability when prioritizing. Priority combines severity with exposure, exploitability and the importance of the asset.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability? Answer: A threat can cause harm; a vulnerability is the weakness it can use. Question two. What does C V E identify? Answer: A specific publicly known vulnerability. Question three. What score range is critical in C V S S? Answer: nine point zero to ten point zero.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name three motivations of attackers. Answer: For example financial, espionage, revenge, ideological, notoriety, extortion. Question five. Which actor type is also called an A P T? Answer: State-sponsored, advanced persistent threat actors. Question six. What is an accidental threat actor? Answer: A person who unintentionally causes harm, such as through a mistake or misconfiguration.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Terms: threat can harm; vulnerability is the weakness; risk equals likelihood times impact. Threat intelligence: feeds, sources (oh sint, commercial, I sacks, dark web), life cycle. Scoring: C V E equals name of a flaw. Actors: unskilled, hacktivist, organized crime, state-sponsored, insider, accidental, competitor, terrorist. Motivations: financial, influence, I P, notoriety, espionage, fear or chaos, extortion, curiosity, revenge, ideological, political, ethical. In the next module, we continue the course.
